title: Running a Design Critique — Structure and Rules
content:
BEFORE
- The presenter states, in writing: the goal, the constraints, the stage of work, the audience, and — critically — WHAT FEEDBACK IS WANTED. 'Flow and IA, not visual polish' saves twenty minutes of misdirected comment.
- Attendees see the work before the meeting. Reading time inside a critique is wasted critique time.
- Set the frame explicitly: this is exploration or refinement. The two need different feedback and mixing them produces mush.

DURING
1. PRESENT (5 min) — the designer walks the work and the goal. No defending yet.
2. CLARIFY (5 min) — questions to understand only. No opinions. This round removes most of the feedback that would have been based on a misunderstanding.
3. FEEDBACK ROUNDS — structured by dimension or by priority, one at a time, so the conversation does not jump between kerning and information architecture.
4. TENSIONS — surface the genuine trade-offs and discuss them as trade-offs rather than as right answers.
5. CAPTURE — the designer summarises what they heard and what they will act on. Not the facilitator; the designer, so misunderstandings surface in the room.

AFTER
- Action items with owners. Every piece of feedback is accepted, deferred with a reason, or rejected with a reason.
- A follow-up only if the work changes materially.

RULES THAT MAKE IT WORK
- Critique the work against its stated goal, not against what you would have made.
- One conversation at a time. A facilitator's main job is preventing three parallel threads.
- Rotate the facilitator so the role does not become a hierarchy.
- Keep it small. Six people is a critique; twelve is a meeting.
- Regular ritual, not an event. Weekly and low-stakes beats monthly and high-stakes.

title: Feedback Language That Lands
content:
THE FOUR FORMS, in increasing commitment:
- 'I NOTICE…' — a neutral, checkable observation. 'I notice there are three filled buttons on this screen.' Almost impossible to argue with, which is why it opens well.
- 'I WONDER…' — a question or exploration. 'I wonder what happens when the product title is 90 characters.'
- 'WHAT IF…' — an alternative offered without insisting. 'What if the shipping cost appeared before the payment step?'
- 'I THINK… BECAUSE…' — an opinion with rationale attached. The 'because' is not optional; an opinion without it is a preference presented as authority.

WHAT TO AVOID
- 'I don't like…' — unactionable and personal. Convert it: what specifically, and against what standard?
- 'Users won't…' — a claim about people, asserted without evidence. Either cite the evidence or reframe as 'I'd want to check whether…'.
- 'Just…' — 'just make it bigger', 'just move it'. Erases the trade-off the designer was navigating.
- Stacked hedges. 'This might maybe be a little confusing perhaps' communicates nothing. State the observation; put the uncertainty in a confidence label.
- Solutioning instead of problem-naming. 'It needs a tooltip' presumes the fix and forecloses better ones. Name the problem: 'I couldn't tell what this field wanted.'
- Feedback on the un-designed. Critiquing colour on a wireframe.

RECEIVING FEEDBACK
- Take notes; do not defend in the moment. Defending stops the flow of information you came for.
- Ask 'what made you expect X?' — this converts an opinion into the observation behind it, which is the useful part.
- You are not obliged to act on everything. You ARE obliged to say what you decided and why. Silent rejection is what makes people stop giving feedback.

title: Design Rationale — Making Decisions Defensible
content:
A rationale is not a justification written after the fact. It is the record of a decision: what you chose, what you chose against, and on what basis.

THE FORMAT, per significant decision:
- DECISION — what you did, specifically.
- PROBLEM — the user or business problem it addresses.
- ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED — at least two, described fairly. A rationale listing one option is an assertion.
- BASIS — what makes this the right choice. In descending order of strength: (1) data from this product, (2) research with these users, (3) an established principle or platform convention, (4) an analogous precedent, (5) reasoned judgement. Say which tier you are on. 'Reasoned judgement' is a legitimate basis, honestly labelled.
- TRADE-OFF ACCEPTED — what this choice makes worse. Every real decision has one; a decision with no stated cost has not been examined.
- HOW WE WOULD KNOW IT WAS WRONG — the metric, signal, or observation that would falsify it.

WHY THE LAST TWO MATTER MOST: stating the trade-off pre-empts the critique that finds it and makes you the person who already knew. Stating the falsifier converts a matter of taste into a matter of evidence, which is the only way a design argument ever actually ends.

WHERE IT LIVES: on the frame, in Figma comments or annotations, next to the decision. Not in a separate document. The purpose is to answer the question at the moment it is asked — including six months later, when the person asking is you.

WHAT NOT TO DO: write rationale for every decision. Write it for the ones that (a) someone will question, (b) cost something to reverse, or (c) you will forget the reasoning for. Ten good rationales beat a hundred rows of documentation nobody reads.

title: Red-Teaming Your Own Design
content:
A red-team attacks the load-bearing assumptions NOW, while there is still time to test the cheapest one. It is not a pre-mortem — a pre-mortem imagines failure and narrates backwards; a red-team attacks the logic in the present.

THE METHOD:
1. EXTRACT EVERY CLAIM the design asserts as true — about the user, the task, the context, the data, the constraint. Then separate LOAD-BEARING claims (if false, the design fails) from cosmetic ones. Only attack the load-bearing ones.
2. STEELMAN, THEN ATTACK. State the strongest version of why the claim might be true, then attack THAT. An attack on a weak version of your own assumption is self-flattery.
3. WRITE EACH FAILURE AS 'FAILS IF ___'. Concrete and falsifiable. 'Fails if shoppers don't understand that the size selector filters availability' beats 'usability risk'.
4. RANK by (impact if wrong) × (likelihood wrong) × (cheapness to test). The top of the list is what you check this week.
5. FOR EACH SURVIVING ASSUMPTION, produce four things: the precise breaking condition, the evidence you could get this week, the kill criterion (the threshold at which you change course), and the cheapest test that moves your belief.
6. SAY WHAT HOLDS UP. A red-team that manufactures doubt is as useless as one that rubber-stamps. Never invent a weakness the design does not have.

TYPICAL DESIGN ASSUMPTIONS WORTH ATTACKING:
- 'Users will scroll to find this.' Cheapest test: a scroll-depth query on the existing page.
- 'This is discoverable.' Cheapest test: a five-person first-click test.
- 'The content will be about this long.' Cheapest test: query the real data for the 95th percentile.
- 'Users know what this term means.' Cheapest test: ask five of them to define it.
- 'This is the primary task.' Cheapest test: look at what people actually do in analytics.

WHY DO THIS BEFORE THE REVIEW: every assumption you attack yourself is one you are not defending in front of stakeholders.

title: Pre-Mortem — Imagining the Failure First
content:
A pre-mortem asks the team to assume the launch has already failed, then narrate why. It works because it converts 'what could go wrong' — which people answer politely — into 'what did go wrong', which people answer honestly. Prospective hindsight measurably increases the specificity of identified risks.

RUNNING ONE (45 minutes):
1. FRAME: 'It is six months after launch. The feature failed. Write down why.' Present it as fact, not possibility.
2. SILENT WRITING (7 min). Individually, no discussion. Independence again is the mechanism.
3. ROUND-ROBIN READ-OUT. One item each, in turn, until exhausted. No debating.
4. CLUSTER by theme.
5. FOR EACH CLUSTER: how likely, how bad, what early signal would tell us it is happening, and what we would do now if we believed it.
6. PICK THE TOP THREE and assign a mitigation with an owner.

WHAT SURFACES IN DESIGN PRE-MORTEMS, reliably:
- 'We never designed the empty state, so the first-run experience was terrible.'
- 'The real data was longer/messier than the mock and the layout broke.'
- 'Engineering couldn't build the interaction and shipped something simpler that undermined the concept.'
- 'It was fine on desktop and unusable on mobile, which was most of the traffic.'
- 'Nobody found it.'
- 'It was slow, and slow made it feel broken.'
- 'The error case was more common than we assumed and it was undesigned.'

WHY IT IS WORTH THE 45 MINUTES: every one of those failures is cheap to prevent at design time and expensive to fix after. And a pre-mortem gives the quiet, sceptical people on the team a sanctioned way to say the thing they were not going to say in a review.

title: Defending a Design Decision Without Being Defensive
content:
THE SITUATION: a stakeholder says 'make the logo bigger' / 'can we add a carousel' / 'the CEO wants it blue'.

THE MOVE, in order:
1. FIND THE PROBLEM BEHIND THE REQUEST. Requests are usually solutions to unstated problems. 'Make the logo bigger' often means 'I don't feel confident this looks like us' or 'the brand team will complain'. Ask: 'What would that solve?' Then design for THAT, which is frequently not a bigger logo.
2. AGREE ON THE GOAL BEFORE THE MEANS. If you and the stakeholder agree the goal is conversion, the argument becomes empirical rather than aesthetic. If you disagree about the goal, no amount of design reasoning will settle it, and that is the conversation to have.
3. STATE THE TRADE-OFF, NOT THE VERDICT. 'We can do that; it costs X' outperforms 'that's a bad idea'. 'A carousel is possible — historically only the first slide gets meaningful engagement, so the content on slides two and three would effectively be unpublished. Which single message matters most?'
4. USE THE STRONGEST BASIS YOU HAVE, AND NAME ITS TIER. Product data > research with these users > established principle > precedent > judgement. Do not dress up tier five as tier one; you will be caught and it costs you the next argument.
5. OFFER A TEST WHEN THE DISAGREEMENT IS EMPIRICAL. 'I think this loses conversions. Cheapest way to find out is an A/B test on the pricing page for two weeks.' Converting a taste argument into a testable one ends it, whoever is right.
6. CONCEDE FAST WHEN THE STAKES ARE LOW. Spending credibility on a border radius leaves none for the checkout flow. Pick the two decisions per project that genuinely matter and let the rest go.
7. WHEN OVERRULED, DOCUMENT AND MOVE ON. Record the decision, who made it, and the expected consequence, without editorialising. If the consequence materialises, the record does the arguing for you. If it does not, you learned something.

WHAT LOSES ARGUMENTS: appeals to authority ('best practice says'), appeals to taste ('it's cleaner'), and visible frustration.

title: Framing Design Decisions in Product Terms
content:
Design arguments lose to product arguments in most rooms. Learn to make the product argument for your own design.

THE TRANSLATION TABLE:
- 'The hierarchy is unclear' → 'Users can't tell what to do next, which shows up as bounce on this step.'
- 'This needs more whitespace' → 'The primary action is competing with four other elements; isolating it typically lifts click-through on the step.'
- 'The error messages are bad' → 'These generate support tickets and abandoned sessions; specific messages let users self-recover.'
- 'We should design the empty state' → 'This is the first screen every new user sees; right now it teaches them nothing and gives them nothing to do.'
- 'The form is too long' → 'Every field costs completion rate. Six of these eleven fields aren't needed to complete the action.'
- 'We need a design system' → 'We rebuild the same components repeatedly and they drift; the cost is engineering time and inconsistency users read as unreliability.'

METRICS THAT MAP TO DESIGN WORK:
- HEART (Google): Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, Task success. Task success is the one most design work moves directly.
- Funnel step conversion, for anything in a purchase or signup path.
- Time-on-task and error rate, for professional tools.
- Support ticket volume by topic — the most under-used design metric and the easiest to get.
- Core Web Vitals (LCP, CLS, INP) for anything web, especially commerce, where they correlate with conversion.

THE OPPORTUNITY SCORE (Dan Olsen), for arguing about what to work on: survey users on Importance and Satisfaction per need, normalised 0–1. Opportunity Score = Importance × (1 − Satisfaction). High importance, low satisfaction is where the value is. It prioritises PROBLEMS rather than features, which is exactly the framing that gives design a seat in the prioritisation conversation.

RICE, for arguing about sequencing: (Reach × Impact × Confidence) / Effort. Its value to a designer is not the number but the Confidence term — it forces the room to admit how much of the plan is guessing.
source: Google HEART; Dan Olsen — Opportunity Score; Intercom — RICE

title: Critiquing AI-Generated Design Work
content:
AI-generated layouts and components fail in characteristic ways. Knowing the signature saves review time.

WHAT TO CHECK FIRST, because it is almost always wrong:
- OFF-SYSTEM VALUES. Spacing, radii, and colours that are plausible but not from the token set. Generated work converges on 16/24/32 and generic greys regardless of your system.
- STATES MISSING. Generated screens are ideal-state only, almost without exception.
- CONTENT LENGTH ASSUMED SHORT. Titles, labels, and descriptions sized to the sample text.
- HIERARCHY FLAT OR OVER-EMPHASISED. Either everything the same weight, or every element badged and bolded.
- COPY THAT IS FLUENT AND EMPTY. Grammatical, on-brand-sounding, and saying nothing specific. Buttons labelled 'Get Started' and 'Learn More'.
- ACCESSIBILITY UNCHECKED. Contrast on secondary text, focus states absent, colour-only status.
- PATTERN PASTICHE. A layout assembled from the average of popular products, well-executed and undifferentiated. This is the hardest failure to name and the most important — it is competent and it is nobody's product.
- PLAUSIBLE-BUT-WRONG DOMAIN LOGIC. In crypto and commerce especially: a fee that appears after confirmation, a variant selector that permits impossible combinations, a balance that animates.

HOW TO USE GENERATION WELL: as a fast executor of a decision you have already made, and as a way to see many mediocre options quickly so you can identify what the good one needs. Not as a decision-maker.

THE STANDARD YOU HOLD IT TO: the same one. If a junior designer handed you this, would you ship it? Generated work benefits from an unearned assumption of competence because it is polished. Polish is the cheapest thing to generate and the least informative signal of quality.

THE ONE THING IT CANNOT DO: know what your users know. Every finding that depends on your specific users, your data shapes, or your business constraints is yours to supply.

title: Design Review Cadence — Quality Gates Without Bottlenecks
content:
FOUR DIFFERENT REVIEWS, four different purposes. Conflating them is why reviews feel useless.

1. DESK CRIT — informal, 1:1, any time, 15 minutes. Purpose: unblock. Best done early and often; the cheapest possible feedback.
2. TEAM CRIT — scheduled, weekly, 45–60 minutes, 4–6 people. Purpose: improve the work and spread craft standards. Exploration and refinement work should be in separate sessions or clearly labelled.
3. SYSTEM REVIEW — before anything enters the design system. Purpose: is this a genuine new pattern or a variant of an existing one, and does it meet the system's bar (states, tokens, accessibility, documentation)? This is the gate that prevents design debt, and it is the one most teams do not have.
4. SIGN-OFF / STAKEHOLDER REVIEW — decision-focused. Purpose: approve, not improve. Bring one recommendation and the trade-off, not three options. Presenting options to a decision-maker delegates your job.

WHAT KEEPS IT FROM BECOMING A BOTTLENECK:
- Define what needs which review. Not everything needs stakeholder sign-off; a copy change does not need a system review.
- Time-box, and default to 'proceed' if the review does not happen. A review that can block indefinitely will.
- Asynchronous first for anything visual — Figma comments pinned to elements, with a deadline. Reserve synchronous time for genuine tensions.
- Publish the standards so review outcomes are predictable. Surprise in a review is a documentation failure.
- Separate the reviewer role from the approver role. Feedback from everyone; decisions from one named person.

THE MEASURE: how often work changes materially as a result. If reviews rarely change anything, they are theatre and should be shortened. If they always change everything, feedback is arriving too late.

title: Self-Critique — Reviewing Your Own Work
content:
You cannot see your own work after four hours with it. These are the techniques that restore vision.

MECHANICAL DISRUPTION
- Flip it horizontally. Composition problems become obvious instantly, because you stop reading and start seeing.
- Greyscale it. If the hierarchy collapses, colour was doing structure's job.
- Blur it. The squint test. What remains legible should be the intended priority.
- Shrink it to 25%. Balance and focal-point problems appear; detail problems disappear, which is the point.
- Look at it on a phone, at arm's length, in daylight.

CONTENT DISRUPTION
- Replace every string with the longest realistic version. Then the shortest.
- Replace the sample data with the ugliest real data you can find.
- Delete the images. Does the page still work?
- Set the language to German and check every label.

TIME DISRUPTION
- Sleep on it. Nothing else works as well.
- Show it to someone outside the project for 5 seconds, then ask what it was for.

INTERROGATION
- What is this screen for, in one sentence? If you hesitate, that is the finding.
- Which single element is most important, and is it visually the most important?
- Which of the ten states have I designed?
- What am I assuming about the user, the data, or the context?
- What did I do because it was easy in Figma rather than right for the user? (Auto layout defaults, a card because a card was already made, a modal because it avoided designing a page.)
- What would I cut if I had to cut one thing? Now cut it and see.
- What will an engineer ask me that I cannot answer?

THE HONESTY TEST: run cr-001's standard pass on your own work and write the findings down as if for someone else. Writing them down is what stops you from mentally excusing them.
